An early study1 reported that menstrual disturbances were associated more often with val- proate than with other antiepileptics among 238 women with ep- ilepsy; 80% of those treated with valproate before 20 years of age had polycystic ovaries or hyperandrogenism. A later study2 found that the occurrence of polycystic ovaries in 105 epileptic women taking carbamazepine or valproate was no greater than that in the general population, although valproate appeared to in- crease glucose-stimulated pancreatic insulin secretion. Subse- quent studies3-5 and reviews6-9 support the association between valproate therapy and reproductive endocrine disorders and met- abolic disturbances in female patients with epilepsy. However, a causal link could not be established since epilepsy itself affects the endocrine system. Symptoms such as hyperandrogenism, menstrual disturbances, polycystic ovaries, weight gain, and in- sulin resistance have been attributed to the development of poly- cystic ovary syndrome (p.2080) in some patients. Other adverse effects of valproate on the endocrine system include dyslipidae- mia, hypocalcaemia, and hypothyroidism. For mention of the effects of antiepileptics, including valproate, on sexual function in male epileptic patients, see under Pheny- toin, p.496. 1. Isojärvi JIT, et al.
